Situation1: The meeting is a routine catch-up that will be recorded for anyone who cannot make it.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I glanced at the clock, my laptop open to the calendar reminder: team meeting in five minutes. As a colleague, I was expected to show up, contribute, and stay in the loop, even if today’s meeting was just a routine catch-up. I knew it would be recorded, but I also knew my manager valued real-time participation. My phone buzzed with a notification from the advocacy group I volunteer with—an urgent message about a discriminatory incident at a local business. They needed someone to draft a statement and start a social media campaign immediately, before the story faded from public attention. My heart pounded. As an advocate, I felt a deep responsibility to act quickly, to give voice to those who were being silenced. But as a colleague, I was expected to be present, to show my commitment to the team. I stared at the two screens, feeling the weight of both roles pressing in, each demanding my attention, each pulling me in a different direction.
